title: Gametes best discriminate natural and sexual selection: a comment on Janicke 2024
content: Here we respond to Janicke (2024) and his new definition of sexual selection. With a detailed analysis of competing ideas, Janicke steers a course between a definition of sexual selection that would blur into natural selection (ie within-sex competition for resources that influence reproductive success: Clutton-Brock 2009), and our recent definition which builds on common practice in the field, but sharpens the focus on to competition for gametes: “sexual selection is any selection that arises from fitness differences associated with nonrandom success in the competition for access to gametes for fertilization” (Shuker and Kvarnemo 2021). It is crucial to remember that this competition is within a sex, even if it is sometimes mediated by between-sex interactions (during mate choice or conflicts over mating). Janicke highlights that we are very specific in what is being competed for: gametes. However, he distances himself from this focus and instead suggests sexual selection is better defined as “competition within a sex for any resources used for reproduction that are provided by a potential mating partner” (Janicke 2024). Janicke's definition may have the appearance of a pleasing simplicity. For Janicke, it all comes down to competition for mates, regardless of whether this involves access to gametes or other resources, or who ends up fertilizing whose eggs.
